title: The Shepheardes Calender
description: Spenser's first major work, published anonymously under the signature 'Immerito': twelve eclogues, one for each month, in which shepherds debate love, poetry, and religion in a deliberately archaic diction, with a learned commentary by 'E.K.' and woodcuts for each month.
plot_or_argument: Through the revolving year, the shepherd Colin Clout loves the disdainful Rosalind, sings and despairs, while his fellows Hobbinol, Cuddie, Piers, and Palinode dispute the duties of poets and pastors; the sequence closes with December's elegy for the dying year.
narrative_structure: A Virgilian eclogue book of twelve parts arranged by month, with framing apparatus (title page, argument, gloss) supplied by the commentator E.K.
principal_characters: Colin Clout; Hobbinol; Rosalind; Cuddie; Piers; Palinode; E.K. (the commentator)
meter_and_prosody: A bravura display of stanza forms and line lengths — from four-stress couplets to sestinas — in a deliberately archaic 'shepherdly' English.
historical_context: Published in the year of the proposed Anjou marriage and the height of the Puritan controversy; its ecclesiastical eclogues (May, July, September) engage the debate over the Elizabethan church.
literary_significance: The manifesto of the new English poetry: it announced Spenser as the heir of Chaucer and Virgil and launched the Elizabethan pastoral tradition.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously as by 'Immerito'; the authorship was an open secret and is uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Hugh Singleton, 1579. Standard edition: The Yale Edition of the Shorter Poems of Edmund Spenser (1989).

title: The Faerie Queene
description: Spenser's unfinished national epic and allegorical romance: twelve projected books of the adventures of knights who embody the private virtues, of which six were completed — Holiness (Redcrosse), Temperance (Guyon), Chastity (Britomart), Friendship (Cambell and Triamond), Justice (Artegall), and Courtesy (Calidore) — together with the fragmentary Mutabilitie Cantos (printed 1609), all moving through the fairyland that shadows Elizabeth's England and court.
plot_or_argument: In each book a knight-errant undertakes a quest under the commission of the Faerie Queene (Gloriana): Redcrosse defeats the dragon and wins Una; Guyon destroys the Bower of Bliss; Britomart seeks Artegall through her founding vision of Britain; Artegall dispenses justice against Grantorto; Calidore wins Pastorella; the whole is shadowed by the giants, enchanters, and false knights of moral and political evil.
narrative_structure: Six completed books of twelve cantos each in interlaced romance structure, unified by the figure of Arthur, Prince of Britain, and by the allegorical design announced in the Letter to Ralegh.
principal_characters: Gloriana (the Faerie Queene); Prince Arthur; Redcrosse; Una; Guyon; Britomart; Artegall; Talus; Calidore; Archimago; Duessa; Acrasia
meter_and_prosody: The Spenserian stanza: nine lines, eight of iambic pentameter and a final alexandrine, rhyming ababbcbcc.
historical_context: Composed across the Armada decade; dedicated to Elizabeth I, with Books I–III printed in 1590 and IV–VI in 1596 during Spenser's service in Ireland; its allegories address the Reformation, the conquest of Ireland, and the cult of the Queen.
literary_significance: The supreme poem of the English Renaissance and the fountain of English romantic narrative; Milton, Keats, and Tennyson all took their bearings from it.
bibliographical_notes: Books I–III, William Ponsonby, 1590; Books IV–VI, 1596. Standard edition: A. C. Hamilton (ed.), The Faerie Queene (Longman, 2nd edn, 2007).

title: Complaints
alternative_titles: Complaints: Containing Sundrie Small Poemes of the Worlds Vanitie
description: A volume of shorter poems on the vanity of worldly things, gathering The Ruines of Time, The Teares of the Muses, Virgils Gnat, Prosopopoia (or Mother Hubberds Tale), The Ruines of Rome (from du Bellay), Muiopotmos (or The Fate of the Butterflie), and Visions of the Worlds Vanitie.
plot_or_argument: The poems vary from the beast-fable of Mother Hubberds Tale — the Fox and the Ape swindling their way to courtly power — to the mock-heroic tragedy of the butterfly Clarion in Muiopotmos, and the elegiac ruins meditations translated and adapted from du Bellay.
narrative_structure: A miscellany of independent poems unified by the complaint-and-vanity theme, in varied forms from fable to vision.
principal_characters: The Fox; the Ape (Mother Hubberds Tale); Clarion the butterfly; Aragnoll the spider (Muiopotmos)
meter_and_prosody: Varied: rhyme royal, ottava rima, and the Spenserian experiments of the translations from du Bellay.
historical_context: Printed in 1591 while Spenser was in Ireland; Mother Hubberds Tale was long read as a satire on Burghley's court, and the volume was among the works attacked by the authorities in the 1599 satires ban.
literary_significance: The chief English monument of the Renaissance 'ruins of time' tradition and the home of the most influential Elizabethan beast satire.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by William Ponsonby, 1591. Standard edition: Yale Edition of the Shorter Poems of Edmund Spenser (1989).

title: Amoretti and Epithalamion
description: Spenser's sonnet sequence of eighty-nine sonnets tracing his courtship of Elizabeth Boyle, followed by the great marriage ode Epithalamion, which celebrates their wedding on 11 June 1594 through the hours of the wedding day.
plot_or_argument: The Amoretti move from the lover's unrequited suit and the lady's proud refusals through reconciliation to the secure mutual love of the final sonnets, which lead directly into the wedding song; the Epithalamion summons the muses, the hours, and the guests, and blesses bride and bridegroom through the day and night of the feast.
narrative_structure: A Petrarchan sequence with a calendrical design (the sonnets allude to Lent and Easter of 1594) climaxing in the 24-stanza Epithalamion, which is built on the canonical hours and the refrain of the echoing woods.
principal_characters: the poet-lover; Elizabeth Boyle (the beloved); the assembled wedding guests
meter_and_prosody: The Spenserian sonnet form (abab bcbc cdcd ee) throughout, followed by the long-lined stanzas and refrain of the Epithalamion.
historical_context: Written during Spenser's courtship of his second wife Elizabeth Boyle at Kilcolman, Ireland, and printed together in 1595, the year after the marriage.
literary_significance: One of the greatest sonnet sequences in the language and, in the Epithalamion, the supreme English wedding poem.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by William Ponsonby, 1595. Standard edition: Yale Edition of the Shorter Poems of Edmund Spenser (1989).

title: Colin Clouts Come Home Againe
description: A pastoral allegory in which the shepherd Colin Clout (Spenser) recounts to his Irish fellow-shepherds his voyage to 'Cynthia's' court — England and Queen Elizabeth — praising the Queen and the court poets, and then turning a satirical eye on the court's vices.
plot_or_argument: Returned from England, Colin describes the sea journey, the splendour of Cynthia and her ladies, the poets he met (thinly veiled portraits of Sidney's circle and of Shakespeare's and Daniel's generation), and contrasts the court's falsehood with the simplicity of the shepherds' life.
narrative_structure: A single pastoral dialogue: Colin's long reported narrative of the voyage and the court, framed by the shepherds' questions and a concluding debate on love.
principal_characters: Colin Clout; Cynthia (Queen Elizabeth); the Shepherd of the Ocean (Sir Walter Ralegh); Hobbinol; the assembled shepherds
meter_and_prosody: Iambic pentameter couplets, in the plain pastoral style of the Calender.
historical_context: Written in 1591 after Spenser's visit to England in 1589–91, during which The Faerie Queene was presented to the Queen; it records his meetings with Ralegh and the London literary world.
literary_significance: The fullest contemporary map of the Elizabethan literary scene and the classic English poem of the court-versus-country debate.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by William Ponsonby, 1595. Standard edition: Yale Edition of the Shorter Poems of Edmund Spenser (1989).

title: Prothalamion
description: A wedding song ('spousal verse') written for the double marriage of the daughters of the Earl of Worcester, Elizabeth and Katherine Somerset, celebrated at Essex House on the Thames in 1596; the poem follows the bridal procession along the river and closes with the refrain 'Sweet Thames, run softly, till I end my song'.
plot_or_argument: The poet, walking the Thames bank in dejection, sees two swans (the brides) float down the river attended by nymphs; the vision becomes the wedding procession itself, and the poem blesses the marriages and the house of Essex.
narrative_structure: Ten stanzas with a refrain, moving from the poet's melancholy through the visionary river scene to the ceremonial blessing of the brides.
principal_characters: the poet; Elizabeth and Katherine Somerset (the brides); the nymphs of Thames and Lee
meter_and_prosody: The Spenserian stanza with a refrain line, lending the poem its processional music.
historical_context: Written in 1596 in the orbit of the Earl of Essex, to whom the poem glances in its praise of Essex House; published the same year.
literary_significance: One of the two great English wedding odes, and the source of a refrain that became a byword of English poetry.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by William Ponsonby, 1596. Standard edition: Yale Edition of the Shorter Poems of Edmund Spenser (1989).

title: A View of the Present State of Ireland
alternative_titles: A View of the Present State of Irelande
description: Spenser's prose dialogue on the conquest and reform of Ireland, written from his experience as a New English planter and administrator: two speakers, Irenius and Eudoxus, survey Irish history, customs, law, and religion, and prescribe a programme of military subjection and re-education — including the infamous defence of famine as an instrument of policy.
plot_or_argument: Eudoxus questions Irenius on the causes of Ireland's disorder — the Irish customs of tanistry and gavelkind, the brehon law, the bardic culture, the Old English degeneracy, and the Catholic religion — and Irenius answers each with diagnosis and remedy, ending with the scheme for garrisoning and resettling the country.
narrative_structure: A Socratic dialogue in two parts, framed as a single day's conference, with set-piece historical surveys and prescriptive argument.
historical_context: Written about 1596, at the height of the Nine Years' War, when Spenser held the post of sheriff of Cork; it circulated in manuscript and was not printed until 1633.
literary_significance: The most sophisticated Elizabethan statement of the colonial programme in Ireland and a document central to the history of English rule there; it has been read ever since as both policy blueprint and confession.
bibliographical_notes: First printed by Matthew Lownes, 1633, in The Ancient Irish Chronicles. Standard edition: Andrew Hadfield and Willy Maley (eds), A View of the State of Ireland (Blackwell, 1997).

title: Fowre Hymnes
description: Four philosophical hymns on love and beauty — 'An Hymne in Honour of Love', 'An Hymne in Honour of Beautie', 'An Hymne of Heavenly Love', and 'An Hymne of Heavenly Beautie' — in which the Platonism of earthly desire is answered and completed by the Christian ascent to divine love.
plot_or_argument: The first two hymns celebrate Cupid's power and the beauties of the beloved as earthly ladder; the second pair, written (the dedication says) to 'reform' the first, ascend through the creation to the love of Christ and the beauty of the divine wisdom enthroned in heaven.
narrative_structure: Two matched pairs of hymns, the earthly pair answered point by point by the heavenly pair in a deliberate palinode.
principal_characters: the poet as lover and worshipper
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal, with an elevated, liturgical diction.
historical_context: Published in 1596 with a dedicatory epistle to the Countess of Cumberland and the Countess of Warwick explaining that the first two hymns were written in youth, the second two in maturity.
literary_significance: The classic English statement of the Neoplatonic ladder of love, and a key text for the devotional Platonism of the seventeenth century.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by William Ponsonby, 1596. Standard edition: Yale Edition of the Shorter Poems of Edmund Spenser (1989).

title: The Defence of Poesy
description: Sir Philip Sidney's treatise in defence of poetry, written in answer to Stephen Gosson's attack The School of Abuse (1579): poetry is the first light-giver to ignorance, the sweet food of sweetly uttered knowledge, superior to both philosophy and history, and the English tongue is fully capable of the highest poetic kinds.
plot_or_argument: Sidney answers the charges against poetry one by one, derives its antiquity and dignity from the ancients and the Bible, anatomizes the genres (pastoral, elegy, comedy, tragedy, lyric, epic), diagnoses the current poverty of English drama, and closes with the famous mocking peroration on the poet's power to make men 'not only to know, but to do'.
narrative_structure: A classical judicial oration: exordium, narration, proof, refutation of objections, and peroration, salted with anecdote and wit.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, in the polished periodic style of the humanist oration.
historical_context: Written about 1579–82 amid the Puritan attack on the stage; circulated in manuscript and printed posthumously in 1595 in two editions under its two titles.
literary_significance: The founding document of English literary criticism, from which the tradition runs through Jonson and Dryden to the Romantics.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by William Ponsonby, 1595, as The Defence of Poesie, and by Henry Olney the same year as An Apologie for Poetrie. Standard edition: Katherine Duncan-Jones and Jan van Dorsten (eds), Miscellaneous Prose of Sir Philip Sidney (Oxford, 1973).

title: Astrophel and Stella
description: The first great English sonnet sequence: 108 sonnets and eleven songs tracing the love of Astrophel (the star-lover) for Stella (the star) — widely read as Sidney's love for Penelope Devereux, Lady Rich — from first sight through desire, frustration, and the lady's marriage to another, to the renunciation of the last sonnets.
plot_or_argument: Astrophel falls in love with Stella at first sight; he pleads, she rebuffs; she marries Lord Rich; the poems anatomize every phase of the love — reason versus desire, sleep and dreams, the stolen kiss, jealousy, absence — until the final sonnets turn from the vain suit.
narrative_structure: A sequence with a genuine plot — courtship, crisis, renunciation — varied by the eleven songs inserted at points of dramatic action.
principal_characters: Astrophel; Stella; Lord Rich (alluded to); Cupid; Reason; Virtue
meter_and_prosody: The English (Shakespearean-type) sonnet form of Sidney's own stamp — abab abab cdcd ee — with hexameter final lines in several sonnets.
historical_context: Composed about 1581–82 in the circle of the Earl of Oxford's and Sidney's London; printed posthumously in 1591 by Thomas Newman in an unauthorized edition, which launched the vogue of the sonnet sequence.
literary_significance: The fountainhead of the Elizabethan sonnet vogue: Spenser, Daniel, Drayton, and Shakespeare all wrote in its wake.
attribution_notes: Uncontested, though the biographical reading as Sidney and Penelope Devereux is a later interpretation, not a fact in the text.
bibliographical_notes: First printed by Thomas Newman, 1591. Standard edition: William A. Ringler Jr (ed.), The Poems of Sir Philip Sidney (Oxford, 1962).

title: Arcadia
description: Sidney's prose romance written for his sister Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke: the 'Old Arcadia' (c. 1577–80, complete in five books or acts) is a tragicomic tale of two princes in disguise among the shepherds of Arcadia; the unfinished 'New Arcadia' (c. 1584–86) reworks the first books into a heroic romance of chivalric adventure; the composite edition of 1593 joined the revised books to the old ending.
plot_or_argument: Princes Musidorus and Pyrocles, in love with the princesses Pamela and Philoclea, disguise themselves as a shepherd and an Amazon to gain access to the secluded royal household; their courtships, the rebellion of the commons, the trial of the princes for the supposed death of King Basilius, and the oracles that haunt the plot drive the action of the Old Arcadia, while the New Arcadia expands it with the wars of the rebel Amphialus and the captivity episodes.
narrative_structure: An interlaced romance in prose with verse eclogues between the books, deliberately organized by Sidney into 'five acts' on the model of drama.
principal_characters: Pyrocles; Musidorus; Philoclea; Pamela; Basilius, King of Arcadia; Gynecia; Euarchus; Amphialus; the shepherds Dorus and Strephon
meter_and_prosody: Prose of elaborate periodic balance, with verse eclogues in many stanza forms at the act divisions.
historical_context: Written in retirement at Wilton after Sidney's withdrawal from court (1579) and revised in the mid-1580s; printed after his death in 1590 and, with his sister's composite arrangement, in 1593.
literary_significance: The most influential prose fiction of the English Renaissance — the model for a century of romances and the direct ancestor of Wroth's Urania and of Shakespeare's borrowed plots.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the 1593 composite text was assembled by Mary Sidney Herbert.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by William Ponsonby, 1590 (New Arcadia), composite edition 1593. Standard edition: The Countess of Pembroke's Arcadia, ed. Victor Skretkowicz (Oxford, 1987).

title: The Lady of May
description: Sidney's pastoral entertainment, written for a royal visit to Wanstead (probably that of 1578 or 1579): a May Lady must choose between the shepherd Espilus and the forester Therion, while the clownish schoolmaster Rombus and the Queen herself referee the debate between the contemplative and active lives.
plot_or_argument: The Lady of May is courted by the shepherd Espilus and the forester Therion; Rombus presents the case for each; the suitors debate in verse and prose, and the Lady — after a comic intervention by Rixus the pedant — gives her hand to one of them, with Elizabeth I invited to judge the dispute.
narrative_structure: A short masque-like entertainment in prose and verse, built on the debate form and ending with the Queen's judgment.
principal_characters: the Lady of May; Espilus the shepherd; Therion the forester; Rombus the schoolmaster; Queen Elizabeth (as judge)
meter_and_prosody: Mixed prose and verse, including singing parts.
historical_context: Performed for Elizabeth I during her progress to Wanstead, probably in 1578 or 1579, when Leicester (Sidney's uncle) was pressing Sidney toward the Anjou marriage policy.
literary_significance: The earliest English pastoral entertainment of the great age and a document of Sidney's courtly politics; it established the genre that Jonson's masques would crown.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; first printed in the 1598 folio of the Arcadia.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the 1598 Arcadia folio. Standard edition: Katherine Duncan-Jones and Jan van Dorsten (eds), Miscellaneous Prose of Sir Philip Sidney (Oxford, 1973).

title: The Sidney Psalter
description: A complete metrical translation of the 150 Psalms: Psalms 1–43 by Sir Philip Sidney, the remainder by his sister Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke, who completed the project after his death — 171 poems in a dazzling variety of stanza forms and meters, the most ambitious poetic translation of the English Renaissance.
plot_or_argument: The psalter follows the biblical sequence, rendering each psalm in a distinct verse form chosen to match its mood — penitential, hymnic, or imprecatory — with Mary Sidney's completion deliberately answering her brother's opening.
narrative_structure: 150 separate psalm paraphrases arranged in biblical order, with the two translators' portions joined at Psalm 43/44.
meter_and_prosody: An encyclopedia of English verse forms: sonnets, terza rima, sapphics, hexameters, and a vast range of stanza shapes, one per psalm.
historical_context: Begun by Sidney in the 1580s, continued by his sister after his death in 1586, and completed about 1599; it circulated in manuscript among the godly aristocracy and was not printed in full until 1823.
literary_significance: A landmark of English devotional poetry and of women's literary agency; its formal virtuosity influenced Herbert, Vaughan, and the whole seventeenth-century tradition of sacred verse.
attribution_notes: The division of the psalms between the two Sidneys is established by the manuscripts and uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Standard edition: The Collected Works of Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke, ed. Margaret P. Hannay, Noel J. Kinnamon, and Michael G. Brennan (Oxford, 1998).

title: Antonius
description: Mary Sidney Herbert's translation of Robert Garnier's Senecan tragedy Marc-Antoine (1578), the first English version of a French classical tragedy: a closet drama in which Mark Antony, after Actium, debates his ruin with his friends and Cleopatra, and falls on his sword.
plot_or_argument: Antony, defeated and despairing, rejects the counsel of his followers, is reproached and forgiven by Cleopatra, and kills himself; the play closes with the chorus's meditation on Fortune and with Cleopatra's grief and resolve.
narrative_structure: Five acts of Senecan structure with choruses, designed for reading rather than performance.
principal_characters: Mark Antony; Cleopatra; Charmian; Philostratus; Lucilius; the Chorus of Egyptians
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse with rhyming choruses, matching Garnier's French alexandrines with English iambic pentameter.
historical_context: Published in 1592, amid the English vogue for Senecan tragedy and the Pembroke circle's literary patronage; it anticipated the Antony plays of Shakespeare and Daniel.
literary_significance: The bridge by which French neoclassical tragedy entered English, and the first English tragedy of Cleopatra.
attribution_notes: Translation by Mary Sidney Herbert from Robert Garnier's Marc-Antoine (1578); uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by William Ponsonby, 1592. Standard edition: The Collected Works of Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke (Oxford, 1998).

title: Caelica
description: Fulke Greville's sequence of 109 short poems, written over some three decades: it begins as a Petrarchan sequence to 'Caelica' and 'Myra', then turns through political and philosophical verse to the great religious poems of renunciation ('Down in the depth of mine iniquity', 'Sion lies waste') with which it ends.
plot_or_argument: The lover's courtship of Caelica gives way to meditations on the fall of princes, the vanity of earthly love, and the corruption of the will, until the final poems renounce the world for God.
narrative_structure: A sequence in three movements — love, politics, religion — recording a lifelong spiritual itinerary.
meter_and_prosody: Varied short forms — songs, sonnets, and stanzaic meditations — in Greville's characteristically compressed, gnomic style.
historical_context: Composed from the 1580s onward by the friend and biographer of Sidney, who served Elizabeth and James in high office; printed posthumously in the 1633 volume Certain Learned and Elegant Works.
literary_significance: The bridge between the Elizabethan sonnet vogue and the metaphysical and devotional poetry of the next generation; its late religious poems rank with the greatest of the century.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in Certain Learned and Elegant Works of Fulke Greville, 1633. Standard edition: Geoffrey Bullough (ed.), Poems and Dramas of Fulke Greville (Edinburgh, 1939).

title: Delia
description: Samuel Daniel's sonnet sequence of fifty sonnets to Delia, with the appended complaint 'The Complaint of Rosamond' (1592): a polished, plaintive sequence in which the lover vows constancy against time and the lady's coldness, and finds his best weapon in the immortalizing power of verse.
plot_or_argument: The lover serves Delia through her disdain, argues with time and death, warns her that her beauty will fade unless his verse preserves it, and closes with the complaint of Rosamond — Henry II's mistress telling her ghost-story of seduction and murder by poison.
narrative_structure: A sequence of fifty sonnets framed as a lover's diary, followed by the narrative complaint of Rosamond in rhyme royal.
principal_characters: the poet-lover; Delia; Rosamond (in the Complaint); Henry II (in the Complaint)
meter_and_prosody: The English sonnet form, handled with Daniel's characteristic smoothness and grave music.
historical_context: Printed in 1592, in the first flush of the sonnet vogue after Astrophel and Stella; Delia's name glances at Sidney's Stella and at the 'Delia' of Tibullus.
literary_significance: The purest Elizabethan expression of the sonnet convention; Shakespeare borrowed from its phrasing, and its complaint of Rosamond founded the female-voiced 'mirror' complaints of the 1590s.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Simon Waterson, 1592. Standard edition: John Pitcher (ed.), Samuel Daniel: Poems and A Defence of Ryme (Cambridge, MA, 1963).

title: Idea
description: Michael Drayton's sonnet sequence, first published as Ideas Mirrour (1594) and revised across five editions into its final 63-sonnet form as Idea (1619): a sequence of farewells — to the lady, to the sonnet form itself, and to love — crowned by the great sonnet 'Since there's no help, come let us kiss and part'.
plot_or_argument: The lover's suit to the lady moves through adoration and complaint to the sequence's famous gesture of renunciation — a farewell to love that is also a virtuoso leave-taking of the sonnet convention.
narrative_structure: A sequence revised over twenty-five years, ending in the 1619 form with its valedictory design.
meter_and_prosody: The English sonnet, in Drayton's plain-spoken, muscular style.
historical_context: Drayton revised the sequence continuously from 1594 to 1619, mirroring the rise and self-conscious decline of the sonnet vogue he had helped create.
literary_significance: Home of the most famous valedictory sonnet in the language and a case study in the Elizabethan sequence as revisable form.
bibliographical_notes: First printed as Ideas Mirrour, 1594; final form in Poems, 1619. Standard edition: J. William Hebel (ed.), The Works of Michael Drayton, 5 vols (Oxford, 1931–41).
